title: Were They Always Denied Burial? — Short B

segments.text: Were crucified people always denied burial?
segments.tts_text: Were crucified people always denied burial?

segments.text: No. The Roman evidence preserves more than one outcome.
segments.tts_text: No. The Roman evidence preserves more than one outcome.

segments.text: A legal text in the Digest says condemned bodies should not be refused to relatives, but it also describes burial by request and official permission, with refusal possible—especially in treason cases. Literary sources describe bodies left exposed.
segments.tts_text: A legal text in the DIE-jest says condemned bodies should not be refused to relatives, but it also describes burial by request and official permission, with refusal possible—especially in treason cases. Literary sources describe bodies left exposed.

segments.text: Archaeology shows burial could happen. A crucified man at Giv’at ha-Mivtar in Jerusalem was found in a burial context with a nail in his right heel bone. At Fenstanton in Roman Britain, another man had a five-centimeter nail through his right heel and was buried in a formal cemetery.
segments.tts_text: Archaeology shows burial could happen. A crucified man at giv-AHT hah-meev-TAHR in Jerusalem was found in a burial context with a nail in his right heel bone. At FEN-stan-tun in Roman Britain, another man had a five-centimeter nail through his right heel and was buried in a formal cemetery.

segments.text: These cases do not prove burial was automatic or easy. They prove that “crucified people were always left unburied” is too strong.
segments.tts_text: These cases do not prove burial was automatic or easy. They prove that “crucified people were always left unburied” is too strong.

segments.text: The responsible conclusion is variability: release, burial, exposure, or denial, depending on place, period, offense, and official permission.
